newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Documents show Zaire camps used to plan Rwanda war.
newsitem.headline: Documents show Zaire camps used to plan Rwanda war.

text.p: Documents found in an abandoned east Zaire camp show how Hutu refugees used U.N. protection to plan assassination attempts against Rwandan government leaders and wage an insurgency campaign.
Hutu extremists, responsible for genocide in 1994 in the months before they fled Rwanda, used Mugunga Camp as a base to buy weapons, train fighters and co-ordinate plans to retake their homeland.

The documents raise serious questions for the U.N. which spent one million dollars a day on the camps and appears to confirm that extremists scorned U.N. rules banning politics or military activity from its camps.

"We are going to have to think seriously about humanitarian intervention and about what we were doing in these camps in the first place," Romani Urasa, UNHCR representative in Rwanda, told Reuters at Mugunga Camp.

Former Rwandan government soldiers and Interahamwe militia fled Mugunga last week following attacks by Zairean rebels. They left hundreds of thousands of documents comprising archives of the former Rwandan defence ministry packed in three buses.
Also in the buses were hundreds of rounds of live ammunition and mortar bombs.

One series of documents from Kibumba camp in 1995 contains formal requests from Rwandan government soldiers to the head of commando operations in Kibumba camp asking for volunteers for insurgency missions into Rwanda.
Dated October 1995 it gives details of a training programme in the camps of Katale, Kahindo and Mugunga, organised by an army colonel in the second military division.
Other documents show plans to assassinate key political figures from the Rwandan government that took power in 1994 following a war that drove more than two million Hutus into exile in refugee camps.
It also showed the level of military communications between Goma camps and Hutu refugee camps in western Tanzania.
In October 1995 $5,200 was allocated to the commander of the second division to buy weapons, uniforms and boots locally, according to another document.
The weapons were hand grenades, rifle grenades, detonators and cartridges. High prices were anticipated because of competition from other buyers in Zaire's north Kivu province.
One document detailed lessons to be held in the camps including ideology, politics, psychological leadership, guerrilla warfare and special operations such as use of mines.

Another accuses Rwanda's vice-president and minister of defence Paul Kagame, the UNHCR and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni of trying to separate Hutus and Tutsis and forcibly trying to starve refugees to death.
A female Interahamwe member named as Stephanie Mukarusanganwa came second in exams after a a guerrilla warfare training course at Mugunga Camp in May 1996.
Mukarusanganwa was second out of 24 people, scoring highly in guerrilla tactics and orienteering but badly in mine laying.
A British-registered company supplied arms to the former Rwandan government during the 1994 genocide despite a U.N. arms embargo, according to the documents.

The company helped to arrange shipments of mortars, rifles and heavy machinegun ammunition from third countries including Israel and Albania in violation of a United Nations embargo imposed in May 1994.
Documents detailed invoices, air bills and arms shipments and asked for payment of debts totalling $1.9 million. The British company could not be contacted for comment.

Britain's opposition Labour Party called on Monday for a government statement on the documents which suggest the company supplied Rwanda for five years including April-July 1994 when up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.
Hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees, many of whom were involved in the genocide, are returning to Rwanda from camps around Goma, Zaire after fleeing in 1994.
